question: Which terms related to overfitting and variance are defined in the machine learning terminology reference?
answer: The machine learning terminology reference in [S2] defines overfitting as "ways to reduce overfitting include collecting more training data, simplifying the model, regularization (L1 and L2 penalties that shrink weights; L1 can drive weights to exactly zero), early stopping, dropout for neural networks, feature selection and cross-validation to choose hyperparameters." Variance is defined as "how much its predictions change when it is trained on different training sets drawn from the same source" in [S1] [S3]. mentions "is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise" but does not define variance specifically.

citations.text:
2. Variance in Machine Learning
In machine learning the variance of a model is how much its predictions change when it is trained
on different training sets drawn from the same source. High-variance models such as deep
decision trees fit the quirks of one training set. This is a property of the learning algorithm, not the
spread of a data column.
The spread of a feature column is a different matter. In scikit-learn VarianceThreshold removes
features whose variance is below a threshold; the default threshold is 0.0, which removes only
constant features.

What overfitting means in practice A model overfits when its training accuracy is far higher than its validation accuracy. The gap between the two (train accuracy minus validation accuracy) is the simplest warning sign. 2. L2 regularization (weight decay) L2 regularization adds a penalty proportional to the sum of squared weights to the loss, which shrinks weights toward zero without usually making them exactly zero. Advantages: it is smooth, works with gradient-based optimizers, and keeps all features. S5.title: Ml Lecture Notes
S5.text: 3. Generalization, Overfitting and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff A model generalizes when it performs well on new data, not just on the data used for training. Overfitting happens when a model memorizes noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set: training error is very low but validation or test error is much higher. Underfitting happens when the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so both training and validation error are high. The bias-variance tradeoff explains this. Bias is the error caused by overly simple assumptions; high-bias models underfit. Variance is the sensitivity of a model to the particular training sample; high-variance models overfit. Total expected error is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance.
